document.title: Afghanistan: Taliban Decision-Making and Leadership Structure (Islama 11233)
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban Biography: The Structure and Leadership of the Taliban 1996-2002
document.note: [Secret] Rare insight into Taliban governance as of December 1997: the movement accepted the increasingly personalized rule of Mullah Omar. Describes four structures: the Inner Shura (23 leaders), Outer Shura (100+ members), Caretaker Council under Rabbani, and the Kandahar-based Ulema Shura. Excised.

events.description: Omar named Amir al-Mu'minin by scholars in Kandahar
Taliban advance on Mazar-i-Sharif, pushed back to Kunduz in October
Omar named Amir al-Mu'minin by a group of Taliban-picked religious scholars.
Taliban captured Kabul and announced Omar as leader of the Islamic State of Afghanistan.
Rabbani joined Omar in forming the Taliban movement.
Wakil Ahmed led a Taliban delegation to the U.S. in early 1997.
Muttaqi recently led a delegation to the U.S. at Unocal's invitation.
U.S. Embassy Islamabad cable on Taliban decision-making and leadership structure.
Taliban advance on Mazar-i-Sharif, with Mullah Dadullah playing a key command role.
Taliban forces pushed back to Kunduz.
Taliban defeated in Mazar-i-Sharif; Mullah Ghaus blamed.
Embassy officer's brief meeting in Kandahar with an Ulema Shura source, who said it has 24 members.
Caretaker Council formed after the Taliban capture of Kabul.

key_claims: Omar is the key Taliban decision-maker and devolves implementation to advisers and the Caretaker Council.
Rabbani and Hassan Rahmani are seen as likely successors, though no serious rival to Omar exists.
Inner Shura has weakened while the Ulema Shura retains some religious influence.
Haqqani is a respected front-line commander linked to Arab and Kashmiri militants in Khost.
Haji Bashir funds the Taliban reportedly via opium.
